analysis.one_liner: Makes community college and public four-year college tuition-free for most students and doubles the Pell Grant.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2021 with 56 House cosponsors, all Democrats, but was never taken up by any of its three committees and died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a federal-state partnership to make tuition free at all community colleges and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges. It would also raise the maximum Pell Grant, extend how long students can use it, allow it to cover living expenses, make Dreamer students eligible for federal aid, and direct money to HBCUs, minority-serving institutions, and underfunded public colleges. It was referred to three House committees, none of which took it up, and it never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students from working- and middle-class families (households earning up to $125,000) would pay no tuition at public community colleges and public four-year universities in participating states. Pell Grant recipients would receive larger awards usable for living expenses. Dreamer students would become eligible for federal aid for the first time. HBCUs, minority-serving institutions, tribal colleges, and underfunded public colleges would receive dedicated funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working- and middle-class students and families

how_it_helps.text: Provides federal grants to states to eliminate tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and for working- and middle-class students at public four-year colleges.
Raises the maximum Pell Grant and lets students use it for living and non-tuition expenses, not just tuition and fees.
Makes Dreamer students — those brought to the U.S. as children who meet education criteria — eligible for federal financial aid.
Funds support programs at underfunded schools, HBCUs, and minority-serving institutions, including more advisors, counselors, tutors, and smaller classes.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants, and participating state governments would cover 25% of the tuition cost plus meet maintenance-of-effort requirements. Tuition-paying students at the covered institutions would no longer pay tuition, so the cost shifts from individual students and families to public budgets.

drawbacks.text: The program requires each participating state to put up its own money: states must cover 25% of the cost of eliminating tuition, and must keep per-student funding at 2019-2020 levels or higher. Poorer states could decline to participate, leaving their students without the benefit.

The federal-state grant program would replace tuition revenue with appropriations, creating a large permanent federal spending commitment (fiscal years 2021-2030 for the tuition grant program) that future Congresses could cut or eliminate.

Private nonprofit colleges outside the HBCU and minority-serving categories receive nothing, and public institutions face new conditions — limits on out-of-state tuition, requirements on faculty hiring, and mandated aid for Pell students — that some would argue constrain how universities manage themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: free tuition for most students at community colleges and public four-year schools, a bigger Pell Grant, and aid for Dreamers would remove the biggest barrier to college for working families. The costs are real: it commits the federal government and states to a large, permanent stream of education spending (states would still cover 25% of the cost), and shifting costs onto public budgets means taxpayers pay for what students used to pay. But the bill never received a vote, so no weighing of actual trade-offs ever happened on the floor; it died before any of that was tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees, none of which ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jayapal introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, and it was referred to the House Education and Labor, Budget, and Ways and Means Committees.
No committee held a hearing or markup on the bill, and no version was ever voted on by the House or Senate.
The bill died without further action when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Universities and lenders that collect tuition and loan payments kept the existing system; no one gained the tuition relief the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Institutions collecting tuition and loan payments

for.name: 56 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored, and the bill's committees never scheduled it for consideration.

industries.note: Free public college would pull students away from institutions charging tuition; the bill funnels federal money only to public schools and to private HBCUs and minority-serving institutions. Students choosing a tuition-free public option are dollars not spent at tuition-charging competitors.
A large expansion of grant aid — including Pell Grants that can be spent on living expenses — reduces the need for students to borrow, shrinking the market for private education loans.

industries.industry: Adjunct and contingent faculty, and tenure-track hiring
industries.note: States accepting grants must commit to moving 75% of instruction to tenure-track or tenured faculty and prioritize converting adjuncts to tenure lines, a significant shift in how universities staff courses.
